questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graphs show the variation of current I with potential difference V across four different components A, B, C and D.

For which component is the resistance initially constant before increasing?
questions.stemText: The graphs show the variation of current I with potential difference V across four different components A, B, C and D. For which component is the resistance initially constant before increasing? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading $R = V/I$ from the shape of four I–V curves.
questions.misconception: Confusing resistance with the gradient of the I–V graph, or reversing the effect of a curve bending

explanation.body: Resistance is $R=V/I$. The initial straight line through the origin gives a constant $V/I$. As graph D bends over, $I/V$ falls and $V/I$ increases.

perOption.A: The resistance increases from the start.
perOption.B: The resistance falls as the voltage rises.
perOption.C: The resistance is initially constant and then falls.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Four identical resistors are connected in a circuit as shown to a battery of negligible internal resistance.

The voltmeter reads 3.0 V.

What is the e.m.f. of the battery?
questions.stemText: Four identical resistors are connected in a circuit as shown to a battery of negligible internal resistance. The voltmeter reads 3.0 V. What is the e.m.f. of the battery? A 3.0 V B 4.0 V C 6.0 V D 12.0 V

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise three resistors in parallel in series with one, then apply potential divider ratio.
questions.misconception: Thinking the voltmeter reads the e.m.f. or splitting the e.m.f. equally between the four resistors

explanation.body: The three parallel resistors have an equivalent resistance of $R/3$ and a potential difference of $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The series resistor has three times that resistance, so its potential difference is $3\times3.0=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The battery e.m.f. is $3.0+9.0=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Uses only the voltage across the parallel group.
perOption.B: Reverses the series voltage ratio, assigning 1.0 V to the single resistor.
perOption.C: Assumes the two series sections have equal voltage drops.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A battery of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r delivers a current I through a variable resistance R.

R is set at two different values and the corresponding currents I are measured using an ammeter of negligible resistance.

What is the value of the internal resistance r?
questions.stemText: A battery of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r delivers a current I through a variable resistance R. E r A R R is set at two different values and the corresponding currents I are measured using an ammeter of negligible resistance. R / Ω I / A 3.0 1.00 12.0 0.40 What is the value of the internal resistance r? A 1.3 Ω B 3.0 Ω C 6.0 Ω D 13 Ω

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two simultaneous equations from $E = I(R + r)$.
questions.misconception: Ignoring internal resistance or using $R = V/I$ for the external circuit only

explanation.body: The potential difference across $R$ is $IR$, so $IR=E-Ir$. The measurements give $3.0=E-1.0r$ and $4.8=E-0.4r$. Solving simultaneously gives $r=3.0\ \Omega$ and $E=6.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Predicts too small a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.
perOption.B: Correct. This resistance satisfies both readings with the same e.m.f.
perOption.C: Confuses the numerical value of the e.m.f. in volts with the internal resistance in ohms.
perOption.D: Predicts too large a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Four identical capacitors are connected to a cell as shown. [Diagram: cell across the circuit; capacitor X in series with a parallel network; upper branch has one capacitor, lower branch has two capacitors in series, the right-hand one labelled Y.] The charge stored on capacitor X is $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. What is the charge stored on capacitor Y? A $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ B $3\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ C $4\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ D $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: Four identical capacitors are connected to a cell as shown. The charge stored on capacitor X is 6 C. What is the charge stored on capacitor Y?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combining series and parallel capacitors and sharing charge between parallel branches.
questions.misconception: Assuming charge is shared equally between parallel branches, or that every capacitor has the same charge

explanation.body: The right-hand network has equivalent capacitance $(1/C+1/C)^{-1}+C=1.5C$. It is in series with X, so it also carries $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and has voltage $V_{\mathrm{right}}=(6\ \mu\mathrm{C})/(1.5C)$. The lower branch has capacitance $C/2$, giving charge $(C/2)V_{\mathrm{right}}=2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. The two series capacitors in that branch carry equal charge, so Y stores $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Y carries the charge of the lower series branch.
perOption.B: Splits the charge equally between parallel branches with different capacitances.
perOption.C: Gives the charge on the single capacitor in the upper branch.
perOption.D: Treats Y as directly in series with X and ignores the upper branch.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A $2200\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is initially charged to a potential difference of 9.0 V. The initial amount of energy stored in the capacitor is $E_o$. The capacitor then discharges through a $4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. How long will it take for the energy stored in the capacitor to fall to $\frac{E_o}{8}$? A 11 s B 16 s C 22 s D 31 s

stemImage.alt: Question 20: A 2200 F capacitor is initially charged to a potential difference of 9.0 V. The initial amount of energy stored in the capacitor is Eo. The capacitor then disc

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that energy decays with time constant $RC/2$ because $E \propto V^2$.
questions.misconception: Applying the exponential decay of V or Q directly to energy (forgetting the factor of 2)

explanation.body: The time constant is $\tau=RC=4700\times2200\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $E=\tfrac12 CV^2$, $E_0/E_t=(V_0/V_t)^2=8$ and $V_0/V_t=\sqrt{8}$. Substitution into $V_t=V_0e^{-t/\tau}$ gives $1/\sqrt{8}=e^{-t/\tau}$, so $t=10.8\ \mathrm{s}\approx11\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The voltage falls to $V_0/\sqrt{8}$.
perOption.B: At 16 s the energy has already fallen below one-eighth of its initial value.
perOption.C: Uses one-eighth as the voltage fraction, leaving one-sixty-fourth of the initial energy.
perOption.D: Treats the energy decrease as requiring three full $RC$ time constants.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor, a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a fixed resistor are connected in series to a power supply. A voltmeter is placed across the NTC-LDR combination. [Diagram: supply terminals at top; thermistor, LDR and fixed resistor in series along the bottom; voltmeter connected across the thermistor and LDR together.] What conditions of brightness and temperature will produce the largest reading on the voltmeter? (temperature, brightness) A high, high B high, low C low, high D low, low

stemImage.alt: Question 22: A negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor, a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a fixed resistor are connected in series to a power supply. A voltmete

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Potential divider reasoning with standard NTC and LDR behaviour.
questions.misconception: Thinking resistance of an NTC thermistor rises with temperature

explanation.body: The voltmeter reads highest when the fixed resistor has the smallest potential difference. By the potential-divider principle, this happens when the combined resistance of the thermistor and LDR is greatest. Low temperature increases the NTC thermistor’s resistance, and low brightness increases the LDR’s resistance.

perOption.A: High temperature and high brightness both lower the measured pair’s resistance.
perOption.B: High temperature lowers the NTC thermistor’s resistance.
perOption.C: High brightness lowers the LDR’s resistance.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows a network of capacitors connected to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance.

What is the total amount of charge circulated by the 12 V battery?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows a network of capacitors connected to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. 12 V 4 μF 2 μF 2 μF 4 μF What is the total amount of charge circulated by the 12 V battery? A 16 μC B 24 μC C 36 μC D 110 μC

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs to identify series/parallel arrangement then combine capacitances and use $Q = CV$.
questions.misconception: Treating all capacitors as in parallel, or charge as the sum on each capacitor

explanation.body: The two parallel $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors give $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. This combination is in series with the other two $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors, so $C_{\mathrm{eq}}=(1/4+1/4+1/4)^{-1}\ \mu\mathrm{F}=1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. The battery circulates $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=(1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F})(12\ \mathrm{V})=16\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Counts only the two standalone $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors in series.
perOption.C: Assumes an equivalent capacitance of $3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, which the parallel-then-series reduction does not give.
perOption.D: Implies an equivalent capacitance of about $9.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, even though the series combination must be below $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A cell of e.m.f. 2.00 V and internal resistance 1.00 Ω is connected to three resistors of 4.00 Ω, 8.00 Ω and 12.00 Ω as shown in the circuit diagram.

What is the current through the cell when every switch is closed?
questions.stemText: A cell of e.m.f. 2.00 V and internal resistance 1.00 Ω is connected to three resistors of 4.00 Ω, 8.00 Ω and 12.00 Ω as shown in the circuit diagram. 1.00 Ω What is the current through the cell when every switch is closed? A 0.0800 A B 0.500 A C 0.629 A D 0.917 A

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Parallel combination plus internal resistance; routine calculation.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the internal resistance or adding the resistors in series

explanation.body: Closing all three switches puts the external resistors in parallel, so $1/R_{\mathrm p}=1/4+1/8+1/12=11/24$ in inverse ohms. Adding the internal resistance gives $R_{\mathrm{tot}}=(24/11+1.00)\ \Omega=(35/11)\ \Omega$. The cell current is $I=2.00/(35/11)=0.629\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Adds all four resistances as though they were in series.
perOption.B: Uses only the $4.00\ \Omega$ branch and neglects the internal resistance.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the parallel resistance alone and omits the internal resistance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A potential divider has a constant supply of 6.0 V, as shown in the diagrams. Which circuit will provide a potential difference between X and Y that can be varied between zero and 3.0V?
questions.stemText: A potential divider has a constant supply of 6.0 V, as shown in the diagrams. Which circuit will provide a potential difference between X and Y that can be varied between zero and 3.0V? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must trace each circuit to find the potential range between X and Y as the slider moves.
questions.misconception: Assuming any potentiometer arrangement gives a range starting from zero

explanation.body: Let $k$ be the fraction of the way the slider has moved from the top of the upper resistor, with $0\le k\le1$. The equal resistors each drop $3.0\ \mathrm V$, so $V_X=6.0-3.0k$ in volts. The potential difference $V_Y-V_X=3.0k$ therefore ranges from $0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Measures from the bottom rail, giving a range of $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Connects X and Y across the supply, fixing the output at $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.D: Measures across the fixed lower resistor, so the output ranges from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$ as the effective upper resistance varies.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Three capacitors are connected in the shape of a triangle ABC as shown in the figure below.

A 5.0 V battery is connected between A and B.

What is the voltage between B and C?
questions.stemText: Three capacitors are connected in the shape of a triangle ABC as shown in the figure below. A 5.0 V battery is connected between A and B. What is the voltage between B and C? A 1.0 V B 2.0 V C 2.5 V D 3.0 V

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must identify the series pair across the battery and share the voltage inversely with capacitance.
questions.misconception: Sharing voltage in proportion to capacitance rather than inversely

explanation.body: The capacitor on AB is in parallel with the AC–CB series branch, so the branch has $5.0\ \mathrm V$ across it. Its equivalent capacitance is $(1/2+1/3)^{-1}\ \mathrm{\mu F}=1.2\ \mathrm{\mu F}$, giving each series capacitor a charge of $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=6.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$. Thus $V_{BC}=Q/C_{BC}=6.0/3=2.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the charge required on the series capacitors for a total drop of $5.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Splits the voltage equally across two unequal capacitances.
perOption.D: Gives the voltage across AC instead of BC.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A cell of e.m.f. $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a variable resistor, as shown. [Diagram: cell $E$ in series with internal resistance $r$ (p.d. $v$) inside a dashed box, connected to a variable resistor (p.d. $V$)] The resistance of the variable resistor is gradually increased from $r$ to $3r$. Which graph shows the variation of the p.d. $v$ across the internal resistance with the p.d. $V$ across the variable resistor? [Graphs of $v$ against $V$, axes 0 to 1.0E: A line of negative gradient from (0.5E, 0.5E) to about (0.75E, 0.25E); B line of positive gradient from about (0.25E, 0.25E) to (0.5E, 0.5E); C line of negative gradient from about (0.25E, 0.75E) to (0.5E, 0.5E); D line of positive gradient from (0.5E, 0.5E) to (1.0E, 1.0E)]

stemImage.alt: Question 20: A cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r is connected to a variable resistor, as shown. The resistance of the variable resistor is gradually increased from

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must recognise $v + V = E$ and locate the endpoints at $R = r$ and $R = 3r$.
questions.misconception: Thinking the p.d. across the internal resistance rises with external resistance

explanation.body: When the variable resistance is $r$, the voltage divider gives $V=Er/(r+r)=0.5E$ and $v=0.5E$. At $3r$, it gives $V=E(3r)/(3r+r)=0.75E$ and $v=0.25E$. Since $v+V=E$, the graph is the descending line segment joining these points.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows both voltages falling together, although their sum must stay at $E$.
perOption.C: Reverses the coordinates of the endpoint at $3r$, making $V$ decrease as the load resistance rises.
perOption.D: Shows both voltages increasing together, although their sum must stay at $E$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A network is constructed using eight resistors, each of resistance $R$, and three switches $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. [Diagram: from X, a top resistor R goes to a central vertical wire (node P); a second path from X goes through switch $S_1$ and a resistor R to a junction M; from M, one path goes through switch $S_2$ and R to P, and another path goes through R to P. From P to Y there are four parallel branches, each a resistor R, and one of them contains switch $S_3$.] Which switch combination will give rise to the maximum total resistance between points X and Y? A $S_1$ closed, $S_2$ closed, $S_3$ closed. B $S_1$ closed, $S_2$ open, $S_3$ closed. C $S_1$ open, $S_2$ closed, $S_3$ closed. D $S_1$ open, $S_2$ open, $S_3$ open.

stemImage.alt: Question 21: A network is constructed using eight resistors, each of resistance R, and three switches S1, S2 and S3. R R R R R S1 S2 S3 X Y R R R Which switch combination wi

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires redrawing a switched network into series and parallel blocks and comparing four configurations.
questions.misconception: Closing a switch adds a parallel path, which lowers resistance

explanation.body: Closing switches can add parallel current paths and reduce the effective resistance. With all three switches open, the left section is a single resistor $R$ in series with the right section, where three resistors remain in parallel. The total resistance is $R+R/3\approx 1.33R$, the largest of the listed combinations.

perOption.A: Closing all three switches gives $R_{XY}=0.85R$.
perOption.B: Closing $S_1$ and $S_3$ gives $R_{XY}=0.92R$.
perOption.C: Closing $S_3$ adds a right-hand parallel path, giving $R_{XY}=1.25R$.
perOption.D: Correct. All three open give the largest resistance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A circuit is needed to turn on a heater when the temperature of a thermistor is too low. Which of the following circuits is suitable?
questions.stemText: A circuit is needed to turn on a heater when the temperature of a thermistor is too low. Which of the following circuits is suitable? A 0 V 12 V heater B 0 V 12 V heater C 0 V 12 V heater D 0 V 12 V heater

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines potential-divider reasoning with thermistor behaviour and diode orientation.
questions.misconception: Placing the thermistor in the wrong arm of the potential divider or ignoring diode direction

explanation.body: The diodes in A and B are reverse-biased. When the thermistor is cold, its resistance is high and the potential difference across it is high. The heater branch should therefore be connected across the thermistor with the diode forward-biased.

perOption.A: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.B: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.C: The heater branch is across the fixed resistor, whose potential difference falls as the thermistor cools.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A simple circuit is formed by connecting a resistor of resistance $R$ between the terminals of a battery of electromagnetic force (e.m.f.) 9.0 V and constant internal resistance $r$. [Diagram: battery of e.m.f. 9.0 V with internal resistance $r$ inside a dashed box, connected across external resistor $R$] A charge of 6.0 C flows through the resistor in a time of 2.0 minutes causing it to dissipate 48 J of thermal energy. What is the internal resistance $r$ of the battery? A $0.17\ \Omega$ B $0.33\ \Omega$ C $20\ \Omega$ D $160\ \Omega$

stemImage.alt: Question 22: A simple circuit is formed by connecting a resistor of resistance R between the terminals of a battery of electromagnetic force (e.m.f.) 9.0 V and constant inte

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Chains $I = Q/t$, $V = W/Q$ and the e.m.f. equation, with a minutes-to-seconds conversion.
questions.misconception: Not converting minutes to seconds, or confusing R with r

explanation.body: The current is $I=Q/t=6.0/(2.0\times60)=0.050\ \mathrm A$. The power dissipated in $R$ satisfies $P=VI$, so $48/(2.0\times60)=V(0.050)$ and $V=8.0\ \mathrm V$. Using $\mathcal E=IR+Ir$ gives $9.0=8.0+0.050r$, so $r=20\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Divides the $1.0\ \mathrm V$ lost voltage by the charge $6.0\ \mathrm C$ instead of by the current.
perOption.B: Treats the current in coulombs per minute as amperes when dividing the lost voltage by current.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the voltage across the external resistor and finds its resistance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Six identical capacitors, each of value C, are connected as shown.

What is the total capacitance?
questions.stemText: Six identical capacitors, each of value C, are connected as shown. What is the total capacitance? A 1 6C B 2 3C C 3 2C D 6C

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise two groups of three parallel capacitors joined in series.
questions.misconception: Confusing series and parallel combination rules for capacitors

explanation.body: Each parallel group has capacitance $C+C+C=3C$. The two groups are in series, giving $C_{\mathrm{total}}=(1/(3C)+1/(3C))^{-1}=3C/2$.

perOption.A: Treats all six capacitors as being in series.
perOption.B: Reverses the series and parallel connections by treating the circuit as two parallel branches of three series capacitors.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats all six capacitors as being in parallel.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A conducting liquid fills a cylindrical metal case to a depth x as shown below. The case has an

The resistance between the case and the metal rod will be
questions.stemText: A conducting liquid fills a cylindrical metal case to a depth x as shown below. The case has an insulating base. metal rod cylindrical metal case conducting liquid x insulating base The resistance between the case and the metal rod will be A proportional to $x^{2}$ B proportional to x C inversely proportional to x D inversely proportional to $x^{2}$

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that current flows radially, so the depth sets the cross-sectional area, not the length.
questions.misconception: Taking the liquid depth as the conductor length

explanation.body: Using $R=\rho\ell/A$, the radial path length $\ell$ is fixed by the spacing between the rod and the case. The area for radial conduction in the key’s model is $A=2\pi r_{\mathrm{avg}}x$, so $R=\rho\ell/(2\pi r_{\mathrm{avg}}x)\propto 1/x$.

perOption.A: Treats the depth as setting an area proportional to its square and makes resistance increase with area.
perOption.B: Treats the liquid depth as the current path length, which is radial.
perOption.C: Correct. The area for radial conduction grows in proportion to the depth.
perOption.D: Assumes the conduction area grows with the square of the liquid depth.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Twenty-five lamps are connected in series to a mains supply. The lamps do not light up when the supply is switched on. A voltmeter gives a zero reading when connected across the third lamp in the set. Which fault cannot be the only one in the circuit?
questions.stemText: Twenty-five lamps are connected in series to a mains supply. The lamps do not light up when the supply is switched on. A voltmeter gives a zero reading when connected across the third lamp in the set. Which fault cannot be the only one in the circuit? A The filament of one of the other lamps is broken. B The filament of the third lamp is broken. C The fuse in the mains supply has blown. D There is a break in the wire connecting the set of lamps to the supply.

options.label: A
options.text: The filament of one of the other lamps is broken.

options.label: B
options.text: The filament of the third lamp is broken.

options.label: C
options.text: The fuse in the mains supply has blown.

options.label: D
options.text: There is a break in the wire connecting the set of lamps to the supply.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs reasoning about where potential difference appears across a break in a series circuit.
questions.misconception: Thinking a voltmeter across a broken component reads zero

explanation.body: If the third lamp’s filament alone is broken, the open circuit carries no current and the intact lamps have no potential drop. The full supply potential difference appears across the third lamp, so the voltmeter would give a nonzero reading.

perOption.A: A break in another lamp stops current through the intact third lamp, giving zero potential difference.
perOption.B: Correct. The full supply voltage would appear across the break.
perOption.C: A blown fuse interrupts the supply, so the intact third lamp has zero potential difference.
perOption.D: A broken supply wire stops current through the intact third lamp, giving zero potential difference.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Three identical capacitors are connected to a battery in three different arrangements as shown below.

Which of the following lists the arrangements in order of increasing capacitance?
questions.stemText: Three identical capacitors are connected to a battery in three different arrangements as shown below. R Q P Which of the following lists the arrangements in order of increasing capacitance? A PRQ B QRP C PQR D RQP

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Straightforward series/parallel capacitance combinations.
questions.misconception: Mixing up the series and parallel rules for capacitors

explanation.body: Let $C$ be the capacitance of one capacitor. In P, the three capacitors are in parallel, giving $3C$. In Q, they are in series, so $1/C_Q=3/C$ and $C_Q=C/3$. In R, the series pair is in parallel with the single capacitor, giving $C_R=C+1/(2/C)=3C/2$. The increasing order is Q, R, P.

perOption.A: Lists the capacitances in decreasing order.
perOption.B: Correct. The order is Q, R, P.
perOption.C: Places the all-parallel arrangement first even though it has the greatest capacitance.
perOption.D: Places the mixed arrangement below the all-series arrangement.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A battery of e.m.f. $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $1.0\ \Omega$ is connected to a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor and $1.0\ \mathrm{mF}$ capacitor.

[The battery and ammeter $\mathrm{A}_1$ are in the supply branch. The $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor forms a parallel branch. The capacitor and $\mathrm{A}_2$ are in series in the other parallel branch. Voltmeter V is across the capacitor.]

What are the readings of the voltmeter V and the ammeters $\mathrm{A}_1$ and $\mathrm{A}_2$ when the capacitor is fully charged?

Readings of V, $\mathrm{A}_1$ and $\mathrm{A}_2$, respectively
A. $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$, $0.8\ \mathrm{A}$, $0.2\ \mathrm{A}$
B. $3.2\ \mathrm{V}$, $0.8\ \mathrm{A}$, $0\ \mathrm{A}$
C. $3.2\ \mathrm{V}$, $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$, $0.2\ \mathrm{A}$
D. $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$, $0\ \mathrm{A}$, $0\ \mathrm{A}$

stemImage.alt: Question 23: A battery of e.m.f. 4.0 V and internal resistance 1.0  is connected to a 4.0  resistor and 1.0 mF capacitor. 4.0 V 1.0  A1 4.0  A2 1.0 mF V What are the rea

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the active loop and accounting for the internal voltage drop.
questions.misconception: Assuming a charged capacitor opens every loop

explanation.body:
Once fully charged, the capacitor has the same p.d. as the battery terminals and the $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor. No current flows through the capacitor, so $\mathrm{A}_2$ reads $0\ \mathrm{A}$.

Current flows only in the upper loop, so $\mathrm{A}_1$ reads $\frac{4.0}{4.0+1.0}=0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. The terminal p.d. is $4.0-(0.80)(1.0)=3.2\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Assigns current to the fully charged capacitor branch.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assigns current to the capacitor branch and overestimates the battery current.
perOption.D: Treats the capacitor as opening the resistor loop as well.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
5 identical resistors of resistance 1.0 Ω are arranged between points A and B as shown below.

What is the effective resistance between points A and B?
questions.stemText: 5 identical resistors of resistance 1.0 Ω are arranged between points A and B as shown below. A B What is the effective resistance between points A and B? A 0.50 Ω B 1.0 Ω C 1.5 Ω D 5.0 Ω

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Identify the three circuit nodes and reduce the redrawn network.
questions.misconception: Reading the physical layout as a series connection

explanation.body: Potential is constant along each connecting wire, so label A as $V_1$, B as $V_3$, and the common intermediate node as $V_2$. Redrawing the circuit gives a single resistor $R$ in parallel with two parallel pairs in series. Each pair is $R/2$, so the two branches each have resistance $R$ and combine to give $R/2=0.50\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This counts only one of the two equivalent $1.0\ \Omega$ branches.
perOption.C: This adds a parallel pair’s resistance to the centre resistor as though they were in series.
perOption.D: This adds all five resistances as though the connecting wires were absent.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graph shows the variation with potential difference V of the current I in an electrical component

The resistance is measured for current $I_{\mathrm{Y}}$ and for current $I_{\mathrm{x}}$.

What is the decrease in the resistance of the component?
questions.stemText: The graph shows the variation with potential difference V of the current I in an electrical component The resistance is measured for current IY and for current Ix. What is the decrease in the resistance of the component? A zero B $V_{Y}$ − $V_{x}$ $I_{Y}$ - $I_{X}$ C $V_{x}$ $V_{Y}$ $I_{X}$ − $I_{Y}$ D $V_{Y}$$-V_{0}$ $V_{X}$$-V_{0}$ $I_{Y}$ − $I_{X}$

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing static resistance from the reciprocal slope of a straight line with a nonzero intercept.
questions.misconception: Taking reciprocal I–V gradient as resistance

explanation.body: The resistance at each point is the ratio $R=V/I$. The larger resistance at X is $V_X/I_X$, and the smaller resistance at Y is $V_Y/I_Y$. The decrease is therefore $V_X/I_X-V_Y/I_Y$.

perOption.A: Assumes the straight line implies constant $V/I$ even though it misses the origin.
perOption.B: Finds the reciprocal gradient between X and Y instead of the decrease in $V/I$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Subtracts the voltage intercept before calculating the ratios, effectively comparing reciprocal gradients.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In the circuit shown, a wire of resistance $100\ \Omega$ is used to make a connection between points X and Y.

[The left branch has two $6\ \mathrm{V}$ batteries in series, with both positive terminals facing up and X at their junction. The right branch has two $800\ \Omega$ resistors in series, with Y at their junction. The branches share the top and bottom wires.]

What is the current in this wire?

A 0
B $6.7\ \mathrm{mA}$
C $7.5\ \mathrm{mA}$
D $60\ \mathrm{mA}$

stemImage.alt: Question 22: In the circuit shown, a wire of resistance 100  is used to make a connection between points X and Y. What is the current in this wire?

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the potential of both midpoints before applying Ohm’s law to the connecting wire.
questions.misconception: Using a supply voltage as the bridge voltage

explanation.body: Take the bottom wire to be at $0\ \mathrm{V}$. By potential division, each $800\ \Omega$ resistor has a drop of $\frac{800}{800+800}(12)=6\ \mathrm{V}$, so Y is at $+6\ \mathrm{V}$. X is also at $+6\ \mathrm{V}$. The potential difference across the connecting wire is zero, so $V=IR$ gives zero current through it.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats a $6\ \mathrm{V}$ source as driving current through a $900\ \Omega$ series path involving the wire, overlooking equal midpoint potentials.
perOption.C: Gives the current through the $800\ \Omega$ resistors instead of through the connecting wire.
perOption.D: Uses $6\ \mathrm{V}$ as the voltage across the wire, although both ends are at $6\ \mathrm{V}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A potential divider circuit with a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is shown below.

[A battery, ammeter A, fixed resistor and LDR form a series loop. Voltmeter V is connected across the fixed resistor. Two arrows point towards the LDR.]

The intensity of the light incident on the LDR is reduced.

Which row correctly describes the observed change on the ammeter and voltmeter readings?

Option | Ammeter reading | Voltmeter reading
A | decreases | decreases
B | decreases | increases
C | increases | stays the same
D | stays the same | decreases

stemImage.alt: Question 24: A potential divider circuit with a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is shown below. The intensity of the light incident on the LDR is reduced. Which row correctly

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify the measured resistor and infer the effect of increasing the LDR resistance.
questions.misconception: The voltmeter is across the LDR.

explanation.body: Reducing the light intensity increases the LDR’s resistance. The total circuit resistance therefore increases and the current decreases. The potential difference across the fixed resistor decreases as well.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the voltage change across the LDR to the voltmeter, which is across the fixed resistor.
perOption.C: Reverses the current change and overlooks that the fixed resistor’s voltage follows the current.
perOption.D: Overlooks that the increased total resistance reduces the current.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
When three identical capacitors of capacitance $C$ are connected to a cell in series, the total charge stored is $Q_1$. When the same capacitors are connected to the same cell in parallel, the total charge stored is $Q_2$. [The first circuit shows three capacitors, each labelled $C$, in series with the cell. The second shows three separate parallel branches, each containing a capacitor labelled $C$, across the cell.] What is the ratio $Q_1/Q_2$?
A $1/9$
B $1/3$
C 3
D 9

stemImage.alt: Question 21: When three identical capacitors of capacitance C are connected to a cell in series, the total charge stored is Q1. When the same capacitors are connected to the

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student finds two equivalent capacitances and uses the same cell voltage for both.
questions.misconception: Applying a factor of three to only one arrangement

explanation.body: For cell voltage $V$, the series capacitance is $C/3$, so $Q_1=CV/3$. The parallel capacitance is $3C$, so $Q_2=3CV$. Hence $Q_1/Q_2=(CV/3)/(3CV)=1/9$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Accounts for the factor of three in only one of the two combinations.
perOption.C: Uses a single factor of three in the reverse direction.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio of series charge to parallel charge.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A constant voltage DC source is connected across three identical resistors Q, R and S, of resistance 50 Ω.

If the source is supplying a total power of 12 W, what is the power dissipated in resistor R?
questions.stemText: A constant voltage DC source is connected across three identical resistors Q, R and S, of resistance 50 Ω. S source R Q If the source is supplying a total power of 12 W, what is the power dissipated in resistor R? A 2.0 W B 3.0 W C 4.0 W D 8.0 W

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the voltage division and square the voltage ratio to obtain the power split.
questions.misconception: Assuming identical resistors always dissipate equal power

explanation.body: Power is $P=V^2/R$, so for identical resistors $P\propto V^2$. Q and R are in parallel and S carries twice either branch current, giving $V_S:V_R:V_Q=2:1:1$. Squaring gives a power ratio of $4:1:1$, so R dissipates $\frac16(12)=2\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Allocates power in proportion to voltage, giving R one part out of four.
perOption.C: Divides the total power equally among all three resistors based on their equal resistances.
perOption.D: Assigns to R the four-sixths power share that belongs to S.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In the circuit below, the reading $V_T$ on the voltmeter changes from high to low as the temperature of the thermistor changes. The reading $V_L$ on the voltmeter changes from high to low as the level of light on the light-dependent resistor changes.

[Two potential dividers are connected across a central battery. The left branch has a thermistor above a fixed resistor, with voltmeter $V_T$ across the fixed resistor. The right branch has a fixed resistor above an LDR, with voltmeter $V_L$ across the LDR.]

The readings on $V_T$ and $V_L$ are both high.

What are the conditions of temperature and light level?

Option | temperature | light level
A | low | low
B | low | high
C | high | low
D | high | high

stemImage.alt: Question 23: In the circuit below, the reading VT on the voltmeter changes from high to low as the temperature of the thermistor changes. The reading VL on the voltmeter cha

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The two voltmeters measure different parts of their potential dividers.
questions.misconception: Assuming both voltmeters measure the variable resistor.

explanation.body:
$V_T$ measures the fixed resistor’s voltage, so a high reading means a low voltage across the thermistor. This requires a low thermistor resistance, which occurs at high temperature.

$V_L$ measures the LDR’s voltage, so a high reading requires a high LDR resistance, which occurs at low light level.

perOption.A: Low temperature raises the thermistor resistance and lowers $V_T$.
perOption.B: Low temperature lowers $V_T$, and bright light lowers $V_L$.
perOption.C: Correct. Both readings are high.
perOption.D: Bright light lowers the LDR resistance and hence $V_L$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A cell with internal resistance is connected to a light-dependent resistor (LDR), a fixed resistor and a voltmeter as shown.

The voltmeter reading increases.

Which quantity decreases as the voltmeter reading increases?
questions.stemText: A cell with internal resistance is connected to a light-dependent resistor (LDR), a fixed resistor and a voltmeter as shown. The voltmeter reading increases. Which quantity decreases as the voltmeter reading increases? A the charge moving through the cell per unit time B the energy transferred to the fixed resistor per unit charge C the intensity of the light incident on the LDR D the terminal potential difference across the cell

options.label: A
options.text: the charge moving through the cell per unit time

options.label: B
options.text: the energy transferred to the fixed resistor per unit charge

options.label: C
options.text: the intensity of the light incident on the LDR

options.label: D
options.text: the terminal potential difference across the cell

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Track how the voltmeter reading, series current, internal voltage drop and LDR resistance change together.
questions.misconception: Equating the fixed-resistor voltage with the cell terminal voltage.

explanation.body: The voltmeter measures the voltage across the fixed resistor, so an increased reading means a larger current by $V_R=IR$. For the cell, $V_{\mathrm{terminal}}=\mathcal E-Ir$. The emf and internal resistance are fixed, so the larger current increases the internal voltage drop and decreases the terminal potential difference.

perOption.A: The charge per unit time is the current, which increases.
perOption.B: The energy transferred per unit charge is the voltage across the fixed resistor, which increases.
perOption.C: The LDR resistance falls as current increases, so incident light intensity must increase.
perOption.D: Correct. A larger current increases the internal voltage drop.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The thickness of a wire is not uniform. As the distance x measured from one end of the wire is increased, the thickness at first increases, and then decreases.

Which of the following graphs shows how the resistance R varies with x?
questions.stemText: The thickness of a wire is not uniform. As the distance x measured from one end of the wire is increased, the thickness at first increases, and then decreases. x Which of the following graphs shows how the resistance R varies with x? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires relating local wire thickness to the gradient of cumulative resistance.
questions.misconception: Confusing local resistance per unit length with total resistance.

explanation.body: For a short added length, $\Delta R\approx\rho\,\Delta x/A$, where $A$ is its cross-sectional area. As the wire thickens, each added length contributes less resistance, so the graph becomes less steep. As the wire thins, each added length contributes more resistance, so the graph steepens again.

perOption.A: Correct. The gradient falls and then rises.
perOption.B: Makes the graph steepest near the thickest part, where resistance increases most slowly.
perOption.C: Keeps flattening after the wire begins to thin.
perOption.D: Steepens throughout, missing the initial flattening as the wire thickens.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows a cell with internal resistance connected in parallel with a fixed resistor and a variable resistor.

[Three parallel branches connect the same two nodes. The top branch contains a cell, positive terminal on the left, in series with its internal resistance, both enclosed in a dashed box. The middle branch contains a fixed resistor. The bottom branch contains a variable resistor, with current $I$ marked to the right and potential difference $V$ marked across it.]

The resistance of the variable resistor is decreased.
What happens to the potential difference $V$ across the variable resistor and the current $I$ in the variable resistor?

$V$ | $I$
A decreases | decreases
B decreases | increases
C increases | decreases
D increases | increases

stemImage.alt: Question 23: The diagram shows a cell with internal resistance connected in parallel with a fixed resistor and a variable resistor. The resistance of the variable resistor i

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires tracking total current, lost volts and redistribution between the parallel branches.
questions.misconception: Assuming both branch currents fall when the terminal voltage falls.

explanation.body: Reducing the variable resistance lowers the external equivalent resistance and increases the total current. The larger voltage drop across the internal resistance lowers the terminal potential difference $V$. The fixed resistor therefore carries less current. Since the total current rises while the fixed-branch current falls, the variable-branch current $I$ rises.

perOption.A: Assumes the variable-branch current falls with the terminal voltage, ignoring the change in current split.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Misses the increased internal voltage drop and the rise in variable-branch current.
perOption.D: Overlooks the increased voltage drop across the internal resistance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Five resistors, each of resistance $R$, are connected as shown.

[Resistors lie on the four sides of a rectangle and on the diagonal from bottom left to top right. X connects to the top-left corner and Y to the bottom-left corner.]

The total resistance between point X and point Y is $120\ \Omega$.

What is the magnitude of the resistance $R$?

A $120\ \Omega$
B $150\ \Omega$
C $170\ \Omega$
D $190\ \Omega$

stemImage.alt: Question 24: Five resistors, each of resistance R, are connected as shown. The total resistance between point X and point Y is 120 . What is the magnitude of the resistance

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The diagram requires several series and parallel reductions.
questions.misconception: Grouping resistors by appearance instead of shared nodes.

explanation.body: The right and bottom resistors are in series, giving $2R$, which is in parallel with the diagonal resistor to give $2R/3$. Adding the top resistor in series gives $5R/3$. That branch is in parallel with the left resistor, giving $0.625R$ between X and Y. Thus $120=0.625R$, so $R=192\ \Omega$, which rounds to $190\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Treats the equivalent resistance as the resistance of one resistor.
perOption.B: This value gives only $93.75\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.C: This value gives only $106.25\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.D: Correct. The calculated resistance rounds to $190\ \Omega$.
